newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus premier warns of inflationary pressures. [CORRECTED 16:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Belarus premier warns of inflationary pressures. [CORRECTED 16:15 GMT]

text.p: The rate of inflation in Belarus in the first four months of this year more than doubled compared with a year earlier and this trend will continue, though more slowly, Prime Minister Sergei Ling said on Wednesday.
Prices in April were 28.8 percent higher than at the end of last year, compared with a year-ago increase of 13.7 percent over the same period in 1996, Ling told parliament.
The inflation figure came two days (corrects from one day) before a union charter due to be signed with Russia. Critics say the small Slav state's economic woes could hurt Moscow's reforms.
But Ling said: "The government is controlling the process of price growth. The growth rate will be lower than at the start of the year but the general tendency will be maintained."
The jump in inflation was caused by recent price liberalisations in the former Soviet republic. "These are unpopular but completely essential steps from the economy's point of view," Ling said.
International lending bodies unhappy with the slow pace of Belarus's reforms have frozen loans, though some smaller arrangements are still being implemented.

But economists see a flurry of contacts between the central banks in Moscow and Minsk and recent liberalisations of currency and price policies in Belarus as signs that the union process is already speeding up reforms.

Ling said monthly inflation in April leapt to 4.3 percent from 2.3 percent in March and increased by 1.3 percent in the first 14 days of May, despite a monthly target of 2.0 percent decreed by President Alexander Lukashenko for 1997.
Russia's monthly inflation rate in April was 1.0 percent.

Ling said the three main inflationary pressures were devaluations of the Belarussian rouble, an increase in the minimum wage from April 1 costing the government an extra 2.5 trillion Belarussian roubles and credits to the agricultural sector of 5.3 trillion roubles.
"This (the wage rise) could cause problems fulfilling the budget close to mid-year and of course it is a significantly inflationary factor," Ling said.
The government would compensate consumers for the effects of inflation by increasing wages.
The bigger budget deficit resulting from this will be partly covered by increasing Treasury bill issues, he said.
But Ling added they would not cover all the deficit as favoured by the central bank, which had said it would increase issues to 4.3 trillion roubles from a planned 2.9 trillion.

This year's budget foresees a deficit of seven trillion roubles with 3.4 trillion roubles covered by central bank credits to the government, which Ling said were issued at an annual interest rate of 6.0 percent.
Ling added the government would not offer state guarantees on credits to businesses in Belarus and that banks should work out for themselves which companies were credit-worthy.
"Banks are demanding government guarantees on investments -- do not build up your hopes, this will not happen," he said. ($1 = 26,700 Belarussian roubles)
